newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - United Biscuits recovery underway.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - United Biscuits recovery underway.

text.p: British food and snack maker United Biscuits, freed of its loss-making Keebler arm in the United States, reported on Thursday it had moved back into the black and said the first signs of recovery were coming through.

UB reported first half pre-tax profits, before exceptional charges, of 44.9 million pounds ($69.83 million), up from 22.9 million. Profit after exceptional costs was 42.8 million pounds against a loss last time of 37.8 million.
A charge of 60.7 million pounds in last year's first half was set aside to cover losses on the sale of businesses.
After the news UB's shares had risen four pence to 206-1/2 pence by 1145 GMT.
UB, the maker of McVities biscuits and KP snacks, is striving to restore profit growth after ditching Keebler and a loss-making business in Spain last year at huge cost.

Chief executive Eric Nicoli said the group had been through some financial pain in 1995 because of the rationalisation, but first half results showed that investment in the remaining businesses was starting to pay off.
"What we committed to doing this year was to return to growth and to deliver a substantial profit improvement...and we think these results reflect that," Nicoli said in a telephone interview.

He acknowledged UB had tested the patience of investors in the past but said some of its strategic investment was starting to show results. The company aimed to grow by getting the best out of its remaining businesses and by keeping costs down.
In Britain, which makes up about 70 percent of group sales, profits rose 12 percent, despite pressures in the food industry.
"Margin is rebuilding and we're seeing growth in all of our businesses in the UK," Nicoli said.
Profits in continental Europe fell 30 percent to 7.3 million pounds. But restructuring of operations and some market share gains are expected to produced an improvement by the year end.
Asian sales rose nearly 30 percent, with sales in China up 41 percent.

But overall results from that region were held back by Australia, where the snacks business UB bought three years ago came under attack from rival PepsiCo. UB's snacks business in the area saw profits fall to A$5 million from A$7 million.
Nicoli said the group expected to deal with the competitive attack and produce a respectable level of profit for the full year.
UB held its dividend at 3.5 pence. Nicoli said the company intended to increase the payout as soon as was sensible. ($1=.6430 Pound)
